title: Your story in three sentences
hookLine: many churches invite people to tell what God has done; it can be very small
last: I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.

lines: CLOTHED, AND IN HIS RIGHT MIND.
cards: A man has been living among the tombs. People had chained him, and he broke the chains. He cut himself with stones and cried out day and night.
Then Jesus comes to his side of the lake, and by the end the man is sitting there, clothed, calm, in his right mind. As Jesus gets back in the boat, the man begs to come with him. Of course he does.
And Jesus says no. Not because he's unwanted. Because he has a job: go home, and tell.
No training, no script, no theology course.

teach.h: GO HOME AND TELL THY FRIENDS.
teach.b: In Mark five, in the King James Bible: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee."
Two things to tell: what was done, and the compassion behind it. A psalm agrees: "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul."

Early Methodists held love feasts, simple meals of bread and water where people stood and told what God was doing in their lives. Baptist and Pentecostal churches often make room for testimony, especially at baptisms.
Quakers sit in silence until someone is moved to speak. Catholics and Orthodox tell the stories of the saints, and many parishes invite people to share their own at retreats.
People who've heard a lot of testimonies say the best ones are small and plain. Not a sermon. Not a before-and-after movie.

teach.h: WHERE I WAS, WHAT HAPPENED, NOW.
teach.b: Many teachers suggest three parts: where I was, what happened, where I am now. Three sentences. It doesn't need to be dramatic.
I was lonely at college; a friend brought me to a Bible study; I'm still not sure about everything, but I'm not lonely anymore. That counts.
So does: I was angry for years; one night I prayed the Lord's Prayer and meant the forgive part; I'm still working on it.
No preaching, no telling anyone what to believe.

teach.h: WHAT HE HATH DONE FOR MY SOUL.
teach.b: Just your story, told honestly, the way the man from the tombs told his.

how: Many churches invite members to share a short testimony at baptisms, small groups or services; Quakers may speak out of silence in meeting, and Catholic and Orthodox parishes often share stories at retreats and in the lives of the saints.

games.q: you've just been healed. you beg Jesus to let you come with him in the boat. what does he say?
o: go home to your friends, and tell them.
games.why: "go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee." his job was his own story, told at home.

practice: Take the one thing you know from yesterday and give it those three parts, each sentence plain, with no big words and no conclusion.
If your story is about God, say so; if it's about a friend, a book or a hard night, that's fine too. Say the three sentences quietly to yourself, and if you pray, offer them as thanks.

carryVoice: Your line: your story counts. Even the small ones. A hundred and fifty days, and counting.
